Scientists Finally Solve the 1,700-Year-Old Mystery of 8,000 Dead Frogs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.
  • Finding 8,000 frog bones buried in a single ditch raised a strange question for archaeologists working along England’s A14 highway.
  • Nearly a decade later, researchers from Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) believe they have identified the culprits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.

Finding 8,000 frog bones buried in a single ditch raised a strange question for archaeologists working along England’s A14 highway. What had killed so many frogs, and why had their remains accumulated in one place? Evidence that the ditch filled within just one year made the discovery even more puzzling.

Nearly a decade later, researchers from Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) believe they have identified the culprits. The frogs were likely eaten by birds of prey, particularly short-eared owls and hen harriers, that took advantage of a landscape transformed by human activity during the Roman period.

Recent findings suggest that the bones were uncovered between 2016 and 2018 during the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme. After learning about the discovery through news reports, Dr. Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth University contacted Dr. Vicki Ewens, a senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, to investigate.

Clarkson compared damage on the ancient bones with patterns documented in previous studies and found evidence that the frogs had been eaten by birds of prey. Although this helped identify the likely predators, it did not fully explain how so many remains had collected in such a short time.

A closer examination of the frogs’ ages offered another clue. Using a pioneering method based on measuring their humeri, or upper arm bones, the researchers determined that most had died young, during the winter of their first year of life. Radiocarbon dating conducted by the University of Vienna placed the remains approximately 1,700 years ago, during the Roman period.

At the time, Fen waters were retreating from the valley, creating favorable conditions for frogs to breed. This would have provided a plentiful food source for birds hunting in the area. Changes to the surrounding landscape may have made the young frogs even more vulnerable.

Short-eared owls typically hunt over grassland, yet the valley had been wooded during the Iron Age. To understand how the environment changed, researchers examined evidence from snails, pollen, and charcoal. Their findings highlighted that substantial areas of woodland had gradually been cleared to create grazing land for livestock.

By the Roman period, large stretches of open ground had replaced much of the woodland. With fewer trees providing cover, frogs would have been more exposed to predators hunting across the grassland.

“We don’t often get an owl’s-eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” stated Clarkson, who led the study.

“The mystery of these frogs has been solved – a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls. These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world – what wild animals were getting up to in the past, and what life was like for them,” he added.

The findings may also offer clues about how people used the valley during Roman times. Researchers suggest that communities may have visited the area seasonally to move livestock between grazing pastures. A less crowded landscape could have provided favorable conditions for hunting birds, although this connection remains a possible explanation rather than a confirmed finding.

What began as an unusual collection of animal remains has therefore helped researchers reconstruct both the changing environment and the activities of people who lived near the Roman Fens.

Sources indicate that as Ewens concludes, “I had so many theories as to why such a large collection of frog bones was recovered from this small feature. It’s been great to collaborate with Paul to finally answer this question. This research shows how even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”.

In a recent development, reference: “An Owl’s Eye View: Human–Animal Entanglement at the Roman Fen Edge” by Paul Clarkson, Vicki Ewens, Owain Scholma-Mason, Ellen Hambleton, Peter Andrews and Emma Jenkins, 17 October 2026, Environmental Archaeology. DOI: 10.1080/14614103.2026.2746302.

Industry observers note that national Highways funded the archaeological works for the A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme. Funding was provided by Bournemouth University post-graduate support grant for material retrieval, researcher travel, and radiocarbon dating.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • According to recent reports, the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

According to recent reports, the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

Sources indicate that in the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

But why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

It has been revealed that crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

But ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception.
  • Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception. Some 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, which eventually evolved into the chloroplast, the specialized organelle that drives photosynthesis in algae and plants. Other eukaryotic cells, of course, took a very different path, giving rise to all animals and, ultimately, the mammalian cells that make up you and me.

Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.

Obviously, most gene transfers in nature move from parents to offspring (fittingly named “vertical gene transfer”), but sometimes cells will acquire traits from other individuals, strains, or even entire species. This is seen most commonly in bacteria that share antibiotic resistance genes, or ARGs, creating troublesome antimicrobial-resistant (or drug-resistant) superbugs in the process. However, other fascinating examples exist, including a parasitic worm that can control its host by swapping genes. In their new study, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Tokyo explored whether a similar process could take place between cells separated by more than a billion years of evolution, resulting in what the researchers call “planimal” cells.

“We wanted to understand whether entire chromosomes could cross the enormous evolutionary divide between algae and animals and whether animal cells could stably maintain and pass on such foreign genetic material to their daughter cells,” University of Tokyo biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga, senior author of the study, mentioned in a press statement. “These questions are fundamental to understanding how genetic material can move across species boundaries and contribute to evolution.”.

According to recent reports, to investigate this possibility, the authors relied on cells derived from the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, along with mammal cells originating from a hamster. Mirroring the primordial event that gave rise to plant life, the researchers allowed the mammalian cell to engulf the alga, after which—surprisingly—cell fusion produced stable hybrid cells. Armed with advanced imaging and genome sequencing, Matsunaga and his team could track how well host mammalian cells retained this algal DNA over subsequent generations. They found that 16.3 million algal base pairs and intact chromosome sequences from all 20 algal chromosomes were retained, and the algal DNA remained detectable through 155 cell generations.

According to recent reports, “Plants and animals cannot reproduce with each other, so their chromosomes are never combined through mating. Yet, we have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal,” Matsunaga said. “This demonstrates that even the vast evolutionary divide between plants and animals can be crossed at the level of chromosomes, without reproduction.”.

Sources indicate that the key to the planimal cells’ survival was the epigenetic “gatekeeping” ability of the host cell to essentially silence incorporated foreign DNA. The authors estimate that roughly 96 percent of the algal protein-coding genes were basically offline, but it’s possible that future studies could detect how to flip this gene switch to “on.”.

Industry observers note that “Our ultimate goal is to activate these biological pathways and give animal cells some of the unique abilities of plants and algae,” Matsunaga added. “Imagine animal cells that could sustain photosynthesis for long periods, producing oxygen while using carbon dioxide to make useful organic compounds.”.

1,000-Year-Old Welsh Legend May Have Revealed the Location of a Lost Roman Fortress

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A medieval Welsh legend may have preserved the location of a real Roman fort, raising the possibility that other ancient stories contain forgotten pieces of history.
  • The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.
  • According to recent reports, the site is mentioned in Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (The Dream of Macsen Wledig), a story about a Roman emperor who travels to Wales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A medieval Welsh legend may have preserved the location of a real Roman fort, raising the possibility that other ancient stories contain forgotten pieces of history.

The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

According to recent reports, the site is mentioned in Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (The Dream of Macsen Wledig), a story about a Roman emperor who travels to Wales. Until now, the account of a camp in that location had largely been treated as a product of medieval imagination. But the archaeological discovery raises an intriguing question: can ancient stories preserve memories of places and events that have been lost to history?

The Dream of Macsen Wledig is one of the 11 medieval Welsh-language tales traditionally grouped together as the Mabinogion. These tales blend history, folklore, magic, and legend, while some people see in them lost myths. Featuring kings, warriors, magicians, and supernatural beings, the stories offer a glimpse into how people in medieval Wales understood their past and the world around them.

The tales survive in two important Welsh-language manuscripts: Llyfr Gwyn Rhydderch (the White Book of Rhydderch), compiled around the mid-14th century, and Llyfr Coch Hergest (the Red Book of Hergest), written toward the end of that century.

Industry observers note that but the stories themselves are older. They had been transmitted and copied since before King Edward I’s conquest of Wales in 1282, and perhaps as early as the 11th century.

Industry observers note that five of the tales feature Arthur, the legendary warrior whose tales spread throughout all of Europe. The Four Branches of the Mabinogi are a group of stories spanning the landscapes of Wales, Ireland and England, of this world and the supernatural otherworld. The remaining two, including The Dream of Macsen Wledig, reshape particular strands of early British history through native storytelling. All the tales offer imaginative accounts of power and political authority.

Recent findings suggest that in The Dream of Macsen Wledig, a Roman emperor falls in love with a woman he sees in a dream. Determined to find her, he sends messengers to follow the route he has dreamed of. Their journey takes them across Europe and eventually to what is now Caernarfon, in northwest Wales.

The emperor is called Macsen Wledig (Macsen the Leader). His character is a literary composite of a number of historical characters, most notably the Galician Magnus Maximus, a Roman general who became Emperor in the late 4th century. Born in a province that is now part of Spain and Portugal, Magnus Maximus seized power in Britain and went on to rule much of the western Roman Empire, including Gaul (roughly modern France and neighboring regions).

According to recent reports, his legacy in Wales is particularly significant. In the popular Welsh song Yma o Hyd (Still Here), first released in 1983, the singer and former politician Dafydd Iwan invokes Magnus Maximus’s departure from Britain, supposedly leaving Wales behind as an entire nation.

The song draws on a powerful literary tradition – that the departure of Rome from Britain, just before the arrival of the English, saw the birth of Welsh identity.

It has been revealed that but the medieval story is not a straightforward account of historical events. Like the song, it blends historical memory with imagination. Its importance lies not simply in whether every detail is factually accurate, but in what the story tells us about how Welsh people understood the past.

The woman in Macsen’s dream is Elen Luyddog (Elen of the Hosts). She is also a composite character, associated with two figures named Helen or Helena – Helen of Caernarfon and Helena of Constantinople, mother of Constantine the Great. Both were 4th-century saints.

In the story, Elen insists that Macsen travel to Wales to marry her. He agrees, and she becomes empress. Her father is appointed Viceroy of Britain, and together they begin building powerful fortresses. Elen asks Macsen to establish three towns: Caerllion (Caerleon), Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) and Caernarfon.

She also asks him to build roads to link them. Sarn Elen (Elen’s Way) is still the name given to the main Roman road complex linking north and south Wales. The story offers a legendary explanation for features of the landscape that people could still see around them centuries later.

Recent findings suggest that one passage in particular in the tale has taken on fresh significance following the archaeological discovery at Y Frenni Fawr hill in Pembrokeshire. Specifically, the moment in the tale which describes Macsen traveling from Carmarthen to the summit of the hill to hunt. There, he establishes a camp known as Cadair Facsen, or Macsen’s Chair.

Until recently, this reference was generally understood as part of the story’s imaginative landscape. But the discovery of a Roman timber fort on the hill, alongside coins dating from the period of the historical Magnus Maximus, offers a fascinating connection between the medieval account and the archaeological record.

It has been revealed that it does not mean that every detail of the story is historically true, but it does suggest that the people who told and recorded the tale may have known about real places and features of the landscape that have since been forgotten. It also raises the possibility that other details in medieval Welsh stories could preserve valuable historical information.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery at Y Frenni Fawr reminds us that the past is not always neatly divided between history and legend. Medieval stories preserve important pieces of older knowledge, even when they have been reshaped over generations. By reading them along with archaeology, linguistics and an eye to the landscape itself, we may discover more about the people who once lived in Wales, the stories they told and how they understood their place in the world. By doing this, we understand more about the world we live in today.

Industry News: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system.
  • Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a major part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Earth is one substantial system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a fresh trick with them: photosynthesis.

Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

It has been revealed that but this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

New research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

The oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

The researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research highlights that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on latest geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide newly introduced constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

Recent findings suggest that they found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

Sources indicate that the second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

The researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

In a recent development, this graphic illustrates the results from upcoming research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that shows how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it demonstrates that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Recent findings suggest that over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

Sources indicate that "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

According to recent reports, this figure shows the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Recent findings suggest that it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work demonstrates that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

According to recent reports, the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

In a recent development, understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

  • It has been revealed that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

It has been revealed that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

It has been revealed that now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Significant Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Sources indicate that instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Massive Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Recent findings suggest that still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

Industry observers note that they’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar claims, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

Why Ozempic Weight Loss Stalls for Some People but Not Others

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why do Ozempic and Wegovy help some people lose remarkable amounts of weight while others see disappointing results?
  • Scientists are investigating whether the body’s natural tendency to conserve energy during weight loss could be an overlooked piece of the puzzle.
  • Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite, and body weight — have become household names and crucial pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why do Ozempic and Wegovy help some people lose remarkable amounts of weight while others see disappointing results?

Scientists are investigating whether the body’s natural tendency to conserve energy during weight loss could be an overlooked piece of the puzzle.

Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite, and body weight — have become household names and crucial pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

It has been revealed that research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.

In a recent development, these medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.

We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially key piece in a complex puzzle.

Research has shown that semaglutide medications can improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar and cholesterol, strength, and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.

We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age, and sex.

Recent findings suggest that energy metabolism may also be an vital piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym, and the everyday act of digesting food.

According to recent reports, when we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis.

It has been revealed that think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.

According to recent reports, changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an key role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.

Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.

We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization. We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.

The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study and remains an open question for exploration.

Industry observers note that at the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter. This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use. This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating, and during exercise.

We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight-loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches.

Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an crucial step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment.

Industry observers note that this will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey.

Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes.

These include improving your nutrition by increasing protein intake and prioritizing fresh foods, such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins like fish and poultry, nuts, and seeds.

According to recent reports, it’s important to eat small portions at consistent times throughout the day, avoid skipping meals, pay attention to your hunger and fullness cues, and choose water as your beverage of choice. It’s also recommended to engage in resistance exercise to support muscle and bone health and achieve the best results.

These strategies may help limit reductions in energy use as the weight comes off.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a newly introduced paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

It has been revealed that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

In a recent development, understanding why this is vital requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that what was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study demonstrated that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Industry observers note that across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

With that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Industry observers note that despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

In a recent development, combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Industry News: The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike

📅 28 Jun 2020 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.
  • Sources indicate that that said, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

Sources indicate that that said, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

To determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

Recent findings suggest that lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

According to recent reports, to test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

According to recent reports, the Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

In a recent development, the Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

In a recent development, since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for fresh detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

Industry observers note that while it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

While I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He indicates it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

In a recent development, the Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for upcoming detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

Industry observers note that because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Recent findings suggest that underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, says that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

Recent findings suggest that the Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Recent findings suggest that both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

In a recent development, while I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

The Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

According to recent reports, it also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

It’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

In addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

It has been revealed that this one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

We tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a new and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

Industry observers note that while shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a big difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

It has been revealed that if you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s important to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to new people.

Most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

In a recent development, most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you plan to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

Sources indicate that the physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

It has been revealed that that said, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you proposal to scan a wide range of environments.

Industry observers note that in general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how rapidly you tire out.

Mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

In a recent development, high-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

In a recent development, lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That mentioned, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced swiftly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

Industry observers note that “Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert states. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”.

Industry observers note that lubbert also noted that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

According to recent reports, finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you plan to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.

#88734. How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1615 w)

How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • North Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for new member orientation.
  • LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.
  • But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

North Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for new member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” noted Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Industry observers note that saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Recent findings suggest that democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

Industry observers note that “Nobody could have predicted this,’’ said David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

According to recent reports, but the Democratic surge was so significant that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown noted, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

Recent findings suggest that the repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

According to recent reports, “Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

In a recent development, womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic concerns. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

It has been revealed that “There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she stated in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

Womack remarked her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” noted Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis noted. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a fresh map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

In a recent development, “North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Recent findings suggest that heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. Fresh Research Reveals Why the Keto Diet Can Trigger Inflammation Instead of Fighting It

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ketogenic diets may affect more than how the body burns energy.
  • Ketogenic diets have gained attention for their effects on metabolism, weight loss, and potentially even cancer treatment.
  • Now, new research from the University of Cincinnati Cancer Center offers a possible explanation, suggesting that the key may not simply be how much fat a ketogenic diet contains, but which types of fat are consumed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ketogenic diets may affect more than how the body burns energy.

Ketogenic diets have gained attention for their effects on metabolism, weight loss, and potentially even cancer treatment. But their influence on inflammation has puzzled scientists, with some studies suggesting they reduce inflammation and others finding the opposite.

Now, new research from the University of Cincinnati Cancer Center offers a possible explanation, suggesting that the key may not simply be how much fat a ketogenic diet contains, but which types of fat are consumed.

A ketogenic diet is high in fat and low in carbohydrates, pushing the body into ketosis, a state in which it burns fat and ketones for fuel instead of glucose. To investigate the conflicting findings, researchers fed mice ketogenic diets containing different fatty acids and tested individual fatty acids in tissue cultures.

“We followed the research data while studying a different aspect of ketogenic diets and found something unexpected,” said David Gius, MD, PhD, director of the University of Cincinnati Cancer Center, professor in the Department of Radiation Oncology at UC’s College of Medicine, and UC Health physician. “Our previous studies have found that all ketogenic diets are not the same, with different fats causing different metabolic changes.”.

“We found that long-chain saturated fatty acids seem to favor an inflammatory immune response, whereas unsaturated and medium-chain fatty acids tend to favor anti-inflammatory characteristics.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers traced the increased inflammation to stress signals from mitochondria, the structures that help cells produce energy, and the activation of immune cells. Their findings, published November 13 in Science Advances, build on earlier studies in Science Advances (2024) and Cell Reports (2025), suggesting that dietary fat sources and other factors may influence the effects of a ketogenic diet.

Although the experiments involved mice and tissue cultures rather than humans, the findings could have implications for cancer treatment. Gius said ketogenic diets may change the environment surrounding tumors in ways that improve responses to immunotherapy, which helps the immune system fight cancer.

A clinical trial is underway at UT Health San Antonio, where Gius began the research, and is expected to open soon at the University of Cincinnati Cancer Center to investigate further.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Ketogenic diets induce proinflammatory macrophage accumulation through long-chain saturated fatty acids driving cGAS-STING signaling” by Sung-Jen Wei, Joseph Schell, Maiko Sezaki, Agne Baseviciene, Wei Qian, Wan Hsi Chen, Rolando TrevinoJr, Prethish Sreenivas, Estrella Sandra Chocron, Haiyan Jiang, Felix F. Dong, Jenny Chang, Alia Nazarullah, Gang Huang, Erin Munkácsy, Nobuo Horikoshi and David Gius, 13 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg5542.

In a recent development, this work was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) grants R01CA257148 (D.G.) and R01CA214025 (D.G.) and supplements to R01CA257148 (R.T.) and R01CA152601 (E.S.C.). This work was also supported by the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT) grant RR20012 (D.G.) and the National Institute on Aging (NIA) Training Program for Research Scientists in the Biology of Aging T32AG021890-20 (J.S.).

#88732. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers
