A Century-Old Pollution Disaster Has Been Discovered Frozen in Arctic Ice

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.
  • It has been revealed that more than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source.
  • Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.

It has been revealed that more than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source. Much of that contamination went unmeasured at the time, but traces of it survived in an unexpected place: Arctic ice.

Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead. The findings also demonstrate how the Earth’s ice preserves evidence of human activity long after pollution has disappeared from the air.

According to recent reports, the study, published November 10 in Nature Sustainability, was led by Joe McConnell and Nathan Chellman of the Desert Research Institute (DRI), alongside international collaborators. The team examined 10 ice cores from Greenland, northern Canada, and the Russian Arctic, finding that concentrations of toxic metals in some locations rose to approximately 15 times preindustrial levels between 1886 and 1918.

It has been revealed that the evidence pointed to the Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, one of the world’s largest copper producers at the time. Researchers estimated that during its peak production decades, the operation released approximately 11,000 tons of arsenic and 4,400 tons of lead into the atmosphere each year.

“It’s pretty wild to think that a single, albeit massive source of pollution could have affected effectively the entire North American continent and western Greenland more than 4000 kilometers or 2500 miles away,” McConnell remarked.

Using historical census records and models of atmospheric pollution, the researchers estimated that approximately 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic concentrations associated with increased risks of lung cancer and other serious illnesses.

In a recent development, people living near the operation faced particularly high exposure. For nearly 30 years, residents of Montana and parts of Wyoming and Idaho experienced arsenic concentrations that met or exceeded the World Health Organization’s current recommended maximum threshold for chronic exposure. The researchers also estimated that 1.4 million Americans and Canadians encountered elevated lead pollution potentially associated with cognitive effects equivalent to a 2.6-point reduction in IQ.

Although the study did not directly measure health outcomes, arsenic and lead exposure are associated with cancer, diabetes, cognitive decline, and heart disease. Pollution settling onto crops, soil, and water could also have created additional risks beyond those examined in the study.

Sources indicate that to reconstruct this forgotten pollution, scientists turned to the Arctic’s natural record of atmospheric change. As snow accumulates, it traps tiny particles carried by the wind, including industrial pollutants. Over time, the snow becomes ice, preserving chemical evidence of conditions from decades or even centuries earlier.

Sources indicate that by comparing metal concentrations across the 10 ice cores, combining them with atmospheric models, and examining historical mining records, the researchers traced the contamination to northern North America. Arsenic measurements, supported by related chemical markers, closely matched Anaconda’s production history, while lead isotope evidence reinforced the connection.

The timing also revealed how industrial decisions shaped the atmosphere. Copper demand surged during rapid electrification and the buildup to World War I, increasing pollution from ore processing. Near Anaconda, damaged crops, reduced harvests, and livestock deaths had already prompted decades of legal disputes.

After the manufacturer installed pollution-control equipment around 1919, heavy-metal emissions declined by approximately 65%, according to the ice-core evidence. Similar technology had been available years earlier, but Anaconda delayed installation for roughly a decade.

The researchers calculated that installing those controls ten years sooner could have prevented another 60,000 tons of arsenic and 24,000 tons of lead from spreading across much of North America.

The Arctic record captures both sides of that history. It reveals how pollution from one industrial site reached millions of people and how changes in industrial practices eventually reduced its impact. Even today, the ice preserves evidence of environmental damage that otherwise might have remained largely hidden.

It has been revealed that reference: “Widespread North American pollution and health impacts from early twentieth century copper production” by Joseph R. McConnell, Nathan J. Chellman, Sophie M. Wensman, Alison S. Criscitiello, Andreas Plach, Dorthe Dahl-Jensen, Diedrich Fritzsche, Kira M. Holland, Drake McCrimmon, Matthew B. Osman, John Sandlos and Andreas Stohl, 10 November 2026, Nature Sustainability. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01975-9.

Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday.
  • Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.
  • But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the upcoming Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the upcoming Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

According to recent reports, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

Sources indicate that “If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he mentioned, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

Recent findings suggest that no challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

In a recent development, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., mentioned voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

Sources indicate that “The cost of living defeated us,” Paul noted. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer noted.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

Space Entrepreneurs Should Look To 16th Century Spice Trade For Inspiration

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.
  • But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability.
  • The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.

But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability. Such was the case five centuries ago, when most of Western Europe was agog over the importation of precious spices from East Asia.

The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.

For centuries, camels had enabled trickles of spices such as cloves, nutmeg, and ginger to make their way into the kitchens of the high and mighty, be they landed gentry or royalty.

Cloves originally grew in the volcanic soils of only a handful of small islands in the northern Moluccas archipelago, author Lewis Dartnell notes in his 2019 book âOrigins: How the Earth Shaped Human History.â And the nutmeg tree appeared on only nine pinprick-sized islands --- the Bandas-further south, Dartnell writes.

Sources indicate that dried nutmeg. Credit: Wikipedia.

According to recent reports, but as early as the late 15th century and the Age of Columbus, middlemen had run up the cost of these rare spices to such a degree that Portugal and Spain, in particular, were in competition for a sea route to the Moluccas. That is, the Moluccan archipelago in what is now Indonesia.

The idea was to travel point to point by sea and weed out a multitude of middlemen along the long Silk Road --- mostly stretching overland from the Black Sea and Mediterranean through northern India to China.

Thus, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan had a novel idea.

Magellan, born into a family of minor nobility and modest possessions, had somehow convinced Spainâs King Charles V that it was possible to reach the eastern riches by traveling west, author Romeu Gaspar writes in his 2026 book âThe Revolution of Magellan: How 500-Year-Old Rocket Science Changed the World.â.

Recent findings suggest that and even though Magellan tragically lost his life en route at least a remainder of his crew did circumnavigate the globe. In the process, they forever changed the course of history, commerce, and human exploration.

Dried spices were a lightweight, high-value, reasonably imperishable product with which to stuff a ship's hold on long voyages, John Keay writes in his 2005 book âThe Spice Route: A History.â The profits were huge; in 1515, the return on such cargo docked at Lisbon was 700 per cent, Keay notes.

Recent findings suggest that by 1520, the income from Portugalâs spice trade provided 40 percent of the Crownâs total revenue, Dartnell writes in his book. Spices eventually became so prized that in 1677, the Dutch swapped the island of Manhattan for the nutmeg-rich island of Run Palau, he notes.

According to recent reports, A 21st century analogy to such commercial exploration might be if by the end of this century, space entrepreneurs were able to extract and then process rare minerals from the Moon or Mars or even accessible Main Belt asteroids. And then in a cost-efficient manner, reap the profits by bringing them back to Earth. Or at least low-Earth orbit.

Recent findings suggest that to that end, NASA Apollo 17 astronaut and geologist Harrison Jack Schmitt has long argued for Helium-3 mining on the Moon. But until someone fulfills the economics of making cislunar Space profitable human exploration of our solar system is likely to lag. That's because throughout history, scientific innovation usually goes hand in hand with someone's quest for a large profit margin.

Sources indicate that A durable commercial reason for people to work in space could give human space science the transportation and infrastructure it needs, Ret. U.S. Brigadier Gen. Pete Worden, an astrophysicist, chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email.

Within the next fifty years at least, the future of scientific space exploration is arguably best served by robotic means rather than astronauts.

Sources indicate that iâd rely heavily on robots for science and give commercial companies a larger role in developing and operating human spaceflight systems, Worden, who directed NASA Ames Research Center from 2006 to 2015, told me via email. NASA should return to its roots in the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) by emphasizing research and technology development that industry and scientists can build on, he claims.

Routine human sorties beyond low-earth orbit are key.

If commercial space transportation becomes routine, agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) could support research that uses it, Worden argues.

Meanwhile, we are left with space programs that for decades have been hampered by both politics and economics and as a result, have limped along in fits and starts.

Over the past 30 years, NASAâs aims for the Moon and Mars have had to survive changes in administrations, budgets, and priorities, indicates Worden. When a program needs agreement from too many people, it becomes harder to take sensible risks, he says.

If humanity can ever succeed in making forays beyond low Earth orbit that are commercially viable in the same way the 16th Century spice trade was profitable, then this new ocean of space-time could be ours for the taking.

U.S. demand for menopause hormone therapy has more than doubled recently

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • women are taking menopause hormone therapy, fresh prescription data suggest.
  • Industry observers note that monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, fresh prescription data suggest.

Industry observers note that monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the fresh study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

The newly introduced study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

Sources indicate that “Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” notes Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The fresh study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not too long ago, making precise angled cuts meant using a simple miterbox—a block with precut 90- and 45-degree slots—and a squat little saw with more teeth than a piranha. Those old-school setups still have their place, especially for ultra-clean trim cuts without tearout, but they’ve largely been replaced by the more powerful and versatile miter saw.

Industry observers note that when it comes to angled cuts for trim, framing, or furniture, few tools match a good miter saw. A circular blade mounted on a hinged, pivoting arm delivers fast, consistent, and precise cuts at a wide range of angles—something handsaws and circular saws can’t replicate as easily.

The best models combine clean cutting power with accurate miter and bevel adjustments, smooth sliding action, and enough stability to stay precise while cutting dense wood. Features like clear cutline indicators, effective dust collection, and easily adjustable fences also make a huge difference when you’re making cuts all day.

Whether you’re building a garden bed or installing window trim, a miter saw is the fastest way to get accurate, repeatable results.

When selecting potential options for the original version of this article, author Alex Rennie, a former residential and commercial carpenter in Newly introduced York City, first put together a rough collection of options based on brands and saw types he had found to be most useful to him over the years. After paring that list down, he put each saw through a comprehensive series of tests.

Paul Smith updated this article most recently with the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 18V Sliding Compound Miter Saw, which impressed him during testing. He is in the process of testing more models and will enhancement this article with the results of those tests when they are available. In the meantime, those models are included below as recommended miter saws based on reputation, product specs, features, price point, and online customer reviews.

Unlike most sliding saws that use rails to slide the blade forward and backward, this Bosch miter saw uses an axial-arm mechanism that eliminates the need for rear clearance. This unique design (also used by this Bosch model) allows the saw to take up considerably less space on your workbench without compromising overall cut capacity.

We loved the lever locks that secure the arm in place during transport (although we weren’t as much of a fan of the saw’s hefty 65-pound weight), and the smoothness of the arm, combined with the rubber handle grip, made this an especially comfortable saw to operate.

It’s worth noting that while the clear blade guard (compared to the black of the DeWalt models) provides a clearer view of the cutline, this saw lacks a shadow or laser line feature.

Full Bosch GCM12SD Miter Saw Review.

What the Skil 10-inch dual-bevel miter saw lacks in refinement—things like pro-level build quality, multiple bevel detents, and high-end dust collection—it makes up for in capability and cost. At about half the price of most major brands, it delivers consistently clean cuts on a stable, well-constructed turntable.

The motor spins the blade up to 4,800 rpm promptly, so there’s little wait between cuts. In use, cuts were smooth along the rails as I cut through 2x12s, with no tearout or flyaway pieces. The saw is capable of bevels up to 48 degrees left and 45 degrees right—key if you’re making compound miter cuts for things like crown molding. There is a preset detent at 45 degrees left—a common cutting angle—but any bevel angle in between is easily locked down via the rear bevel knob. Even so, it proved accurate across those settings—I had no trouble dialing in compound miters—cuts that employ both miter and bevel cuts—for crown molding that lined up cleanly from both sides.

It has been revealed that ergonomics are a highlight. The trigger sits naturally within the grip, and it’s the only saw I tested that feels equally comfortable left- or right-handed. That might seem minor, but when you’re stretched out on a tricky compound cut, being able to switch hands makes a real difference. Finally, at less than 50 pounds, this saw is no trouble to move around your yard during setup changes or throw in your truck at the end of the day.

Full Skil 10-inch Miter Saw Review.

Recent findings suggest that this dual-bevel, 10-inch saw packs a lot of power and features into one relatively small and comparatively inexpensive package. With nine positive miter stops and a cutting capacity of 12 inches on the bed, you’ll get up to 500 cuts on a single battery charge.

Industry observers note that LED line indicators ensure precision, and a bevel pivot that's as easy to access as it is to operate rounds out this saw's top features. While it's not the most powerful saw, even compared to other cordless options, this one holds its own among the arguably bigger names that populate this list in every other way.

This DeWalt miter saw provides serious power and performance. We found that it maintained speed and power really well during our cut tests, but because it’s cordless, you don’t need to sacrifice mobility when you’re working with it.

The included stabilizer bar ensured that the saw felt sturdy and stable while we cut, and the included LED work light created a convenient, precise shadow line to maximize accuracy. We also appreciated how well the instruction manual walked us through all the different operations, giving us comprehensive instructions on a variety of cuts.

Industry observers note that at a little over 50 pounds (without the 20-volt battery, which you’ll have to buy separately) and with a top-mounted carrying handle, this was one of the easier saws to transport during testing. Plus, this saw’s dust port was located on the side, instead of the rear, which made it easier to fit on a smaller workbench.

With dual-bevel capabilities, smooth gliding rails, and user-friendly controls and adjustment knobs, this cordless powerhouse handles everything from 13.5-inch-wide cuts to 6.5-inch-tall baseboards.

This saw won’t be your go-to if you’re working with large lumber. Nothing bigger than a 2x4 is recommended here, but if that type of work isn’t on your horizon, this saw is as easy to maneuver as it is to operate.

It has been revealed that its small size and extremely accurate blade make it ideal for using indoors to cut trim, flooring, and picture framing. And at just over 14 pounds, it’s a breeze to move from room to room as you work. We also like the gooseneck type of LED built into the blade housing for throwing light on your entire cut. And the 64-tooth blade delivers a clean, precise cut every time.

If you believe you get what you pay for, this Makita 8-1/2-inch miter saw makes the case. Tools should solve problems—and this one addresses a substantial one in its category: size versus capability. A 12-inch saw powers through 4x4s but is heavy and space-hungry; a compact 6-inch is portable but limited. This Makita saw lands squarely in between.

In a recent development, this 40-volt cordless saw delivers corded-level power in a lighter package—roughly 10 to 20 pounds less than larger models—while still handling 12-inch crosscuts. Its forward-facing rails save valuable workspace, letting it sit flush against a wall without the usual rear clearance.

Build quality stands out immediately. The heavy aluminum turntable feels rigid under load, with precise detents that lock in smoothly at common angles—no fighting to find your mark. Preset bevel stops on both sides add convenience, and the front-mounted bevel lock means no awkward reaching over the saw.

Makita also includes dual dust collection options: a standard bag or a ducted port for a dedicated system. Pair it with Makita’s AWS technology and pulling the trigger wirelessly activates a compatible vacuum—an easy, thoughtful upgrade for shop workflow.

Prior to using this saw, I read that some users had complications with the out-of-the-box accuracy of the table in relation to the blade. This situation is problematic when cutting trim, for instance, because it needs to fit perfectly.

Recent findings suggest that I personally experienced none of that. I cut a variety of woods with this saw—from 2x10s to MDF trim—and the results completely satisfied me. Cuts were clean, splinter-free, and above all, accurate at connection.

The saw is powerful, thanks in part to its brushless motor and impressive battery, which Milwaukee claims makes 330 cuts per charge, but I honestly ran out of wood before that number (and according to the battery indicators, I still had half a charge remaining).

According to recent reports, milwaukee puts a lot of effort into getting its shadow line system clear and precise, and I appreciate that when it comes to eyeing up my cuts. As an added bonus, I find the LED field is the best of any saw I’ve used, cordless or otherwise. My only complaints are that the rear bevel is a little clunky to maneuver and the table extenders have an underwhelming feel to them. If you’re expanding your Milwaukee cordless platform, this saw is a great add.

A few of our readers gave us grief earlier this year for overlooking Evolution’s jobsite table saw on our list of the best table saws, so I called one in. I ran a piece of old angle iron through it before proceeding to cut hardwood, plywood, and pine trim with minimal tearout. My takeaway was that the saw lived up to the hype. Now, I’m curious how Evolution’s 10-inch miter saw handles the same materials.

According to recent reports, I’ll start with framing lumber and trim to see how accurately the saw repeats miters and how cleanly it cuts in both bevel directions. Then, I’ll cut some aluminum angle stock and light-gauge steel tubing before moving on to hardwood with the same blade. I want to see how much cleanup each piece of metal needs and whether that last pair of hardwood miters fits together as neatly as the first pair of standard lumber and pine base molding. All throughout, I’ll be looking at standard saw features, as well, including motor power, build quality, table detents, LED lighting or shadow lines, and dust collection.

Sources indicate that the three main types of miter saws are compound, dual compound, and sliding. Each variation performs specific functions and cuts better than the others, so it’s notable that you understand their differences and also have a decent idea of how you strategy on using your saw.

In addition to lowering straight down for perpendicular crosscuts, the blade of a compound miter saw also pivots from side to side for angled “miter” cuts, and it tilts to one side for bevel cuts. A “compound” cut utilizes both of these functions in one motion and is commonly used to create things like picture frames or to cut crown molding for installation.

According to recent reports, instead of tilting to only one side for bevel cuts, dual compound saws (also called “double” or “double-bevel” compound saws) tilt in both directions. This makes work much faster than using a standard compound saw because while a compound saw technically makes all the same cuts as a dual compound saw, its single-bevel design means you spend more time flipping workpieces around to cut opposite angles.

These two non-sliding types are solid options for homeowners who want a reasonably compact and portable machine.

A standard compound miter saw drops straight down onto the board. It’s great for narrow stock but limited by the diameter of the blade. A sliding compound miter saw adds rails that let the blade travel forward and backward during the course of the cut. This feature dramatically increases the width of material the saw can handle—making it possible to cut wider boards in a single pass. If you’re cutting a lot of shelving, flooring, or wide trim, a sliding miter saw, such as the DeWalt 20V MAX XR Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, is usually worth the extra cost and size.

When shopping for a miter saw, you’ll also need to decide what type of power source you prefer.

Recent findings suggest that cordless miter saws have improved dramatically over the last few years, mostly due to the evolution of high-capacity lithium-ion batteries and the inclusion of brushless motors. Today’s 18- and 20-volt models offer plenty of power for trim work and general carpentry without sacrificing the portability that makes cordless power tools appealing in the first place.

I like knowing I can set up the saw anywhere and get to work without worrying about finding power or running an extension cord through an open door or window. That said, corded saws still hold the edge when it comes to cutting ability and run time.

Most miter saws come with 10- or 12-inch blades, and that difference has a big impact on what type of cuts and tasks the saw excels at.

A 10-inch saw, such as the Metabo HPT Single Bevel Compound Miter Saw, is typically lighter and easier to move around your shop or from room to room. It’s more than capable of cutting trim, flooring, and smaller dimensional lumber.

Sources indicate that A 12-inch saw, on the other hand, gives you significantly more cutting capacity—especially when you’re working with wider boards or tall trim pieces like crown molding. 12-inch saws, like our Best Overall choice, the Bosch GCM12SD Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, are a bit more awkward to move around the workplace.

A large saw also adds bulk and takes up more room in the shop or truck. But the trade-off to those negatives is that you’re far less likely to run into a job that you simply can’t handle. I’d rather deal with the extra footprint than discover upon starting a project that my saw is undersized. If you have the space, it’s often better to size up.

It has been revealed that blade speed, measured in rpm (revolutions per minute), is another notable performance indicator. Most miter saws operate between 3,000 and 5,500 rpm, and naturally, higher speeds increase your cutting efficiency. Some saws, like the Hilti Nuron 22V miter saw, even allow you to customize your speed to a specific task, which makes it uniquely versatile.

That said, the relationship between the saw blade diameter and rpm makes comparing the speed of two miter saws a little more complex. Two saws running at the same rpm, but using different-sized blades—let’s say 7¼-inch and 12-inch—will not cut at the same speed. That’s because even though the center of each blade is spinning at the same speed, the outer edge of the 12-inch blade will turn faster than the edge of the 7¼-inch one.

Things get even more complicated when we bring the blade’s tooth count into the mix, with higher-tooth blades reducing speed. As a beginner, you can drive yourself a little crazy trying to determine the perfect combination of blade factors, so I’d recommend relying on your saw’s instruction manual for basic guidance.

Modern miter saws often include features designed to help you cut more accurately and consistently. Some use laser guides to project the cut line, while others use LED systems that cast a shadow from the blade, so you can see exactly where it will land. Detents at common angle stops around the saw table—like 22.5 degrees and 45 degrees—also make it faster to dial in repeated cuts. These features aren’t essential, but they make a noticeable difference when you’re making dozens of cuts in a row.

Chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

It has been revealed that rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, stated legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

Sources indicate that “Yes, absolutely,” she noted when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, stated she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses revealed a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack stated she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she remarked when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”.

Recent findings suggest that leger Fernández noted if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

Recent findings suggest that “We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

Even if you don’t have the means to install a fully ducted HVAC system in your home, you can still upgrade to a more powerful cooling system with a ductless air conditioner.

It has been revealed that ductless air conditioners, often called mini-splits, cool targeted areas of your home without relying on the ductwork. Instead, they connect a compact outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers, which are usually mounted on a wall or ceiling.

Industry observers note that to help narrow down the best ductless air conditioners, I compared models across capacity, efficiency, installation requirements, noise level, smart features, and overall value. I also spoke with HVAC expert Kim Lincoln, who has 25 years of industry experience, for guidance on how mini-splits work, when they make sense, and what shoppers should know before buying.

To ensure that our list of ductless air conditioners caters to a wide range of needs, I looked at units from well-respected brands like Pioneer and Senville and selected models of various sizes at different prices. Many come with features like programmability, dehumidification settings, and, in a few instances, smartphone functionality.

In a recent development, as an added perk, most of these contraptions also double as heaters—which is useful during cooler months. I leaned on my experience with different types of cooling units, as well as product specs I reviewed during my research. The final list below represents the best in each category, including best budget and best for DIY installation.

It has been revealed that for this update, I relied on the expertise of Lincoln, as well as my own experiences with several types of ductless air conditioners. I asked her a variety of questions about mini-splits, touching on topics like the differences between this type of air conditioner from other units, installation, and more. I also updated the products I recommend to reflect recent advances in smart home technology and energy efficiency.

This highly-rated AC unit from Senville comes in a number of sizes, ranging from 9,000 BTUs all the way up to 30,000 BTUs, and it comes in 120- and 230-volt models. Compared to window or portable air conditioners, ductless systems are more permanent, more powerful, and typically quieter. They also give you more control over specific rooms, so you can cool the spaces you actually use instead of the whole house at once. There are some drawbacks, though.

Ductless ACs run pricey (even setting aside the cost of installation). They’re also more visible than central air vents, and you need to size and place them carefully to cool a room evenly. DIY installs or wrong-sized units can cause issues in the long run.

Maintenance can also be difficult, as not all HVAC professionals are familiar with these products. However, for an older home with radiator heat (like mine is), it’s the best way to add efficient air conditioning without blocking most of our windows.

Industry observers note that first, decide how many indoor units you need and where you’ll place them. Unlike window units, mini-split systems are permanent fixtures, so carefully consider where they’ll be most efficient within your home.

Generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

It’s also essential to select a unit that’s powerful enough for the room it’s in—too small and it may not cool your space. The cooling capacity of air conditioners is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTUs, per hour.

As a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

According to recent reports, it’s also vital to consider the electrical system in the area you blueprint to install the mini-split. Many larger mini-splits require 208- to 230-volt power, which works with both commercial 208V electrical service and the 240V circuits typically used for major appliances in homes, while smaller systems may run on standard 120V outlets without any needed upgrades.

Recent findings suggest that quieter units are more desirable for bedrooms, living rooms, and nurseries, where a peaceful environment is essential. Look for ductless air conditioners with noise levels between 19 and 30 decibels, since this range can be compared to the sound of leaves rustling or a soft whisper.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

While shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

In a recent development, A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

In a recent development, mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you plan to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

They’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, says Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

Instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

These systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”.

Recent findings suggest that yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” claims Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

Both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

It has been revealed that some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that concern without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

“Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”.

Some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

According to recent reports, smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is notable for talking, too.

According to recent reports, data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, claims neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

Sources indicate that A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The fresh research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Industry observers note that scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” noted Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

In a recent development, electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

It has been revealed that some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva mentioned. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

Sources indicate that california Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

In a recent development, the race was reshaped by the Golden State’s newly introduced voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

In a recent development, the rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

Industry observers note that in her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she mentioned in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that the race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

Industry observers note that one incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

According to recent reports, two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.
