💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the dairy industry’s “Milk.
  • “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, mentioned in a statement.
  • In a recent development, to test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

“When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, mentioned in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”.

In a recent development, to test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

In China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

It has been revealed that trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan stated. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

Industry observers note that in Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

According to recent reports, women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

Industry observers note that “Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” said Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, newly introduced, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”.

Industry observers note that europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” said Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”.

Sources indicate that tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

Industry News: Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A new map offers surprises

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation plans based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.
  • Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.
  • A newly introduced global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation plans based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.

Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.

A newly introduced global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.

A team led from McGill University analyzed 21,490 species and found that freshwater threat hotspots often differ from those on land.

For the threats compared, freshwater mammals generally faced greater pressure than land mammals, with a smaller gap for reptiles.

Christophe Brabant, a doctoral student in biology at McGill University, led the work with biology professor Lars Lønsmann Iversen, a member of McGill’s Bieler School of Environment.

The researchers drew on expert assessments to identify the threats facing each species.

They combined those assessments with species’ known ranges to map where the threats are most likely to affect them.

The researchers identified three threats that were especially widespread.

According to recent reports, across river sub-basins worldwide, they estimated that each affected roughly one in four freshwater species present, on average. Farmland growing crops came first.

Dams and other water management came second, and runoff from farms and forestry third.

It has been revealed that europe and northwestern Africa’s Maghreb region carry the heaviest combined load of all 45 threats. In Europe, the dominant problem is pollution from cities, farms and industry.

In the Maghreb it is pollution plus dams and heavy water use. Other hot spots include the Nile, the Niger Delta and the Rift Valley lakes of East Africa.

The lightest loads are where few people live, in Siberia and northern Canada, and in the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts.

It has been revealed that global averages hide major differences between animals. Fish are mainly hit by fishing across 37% of their range and by dams across another 30.5%.

Farming was the leading threat across 45.8% of amphibians’ combined range and 31.45% of the combined range of dragonflies and damselflies.

The authors linked this pattern to the animals’ reliance on both land and water at different stages of life.

According to recent reports, freshwater reptiles and mammals face a different enemy. Hunting and other direct use are the main threat across 37.8% of reptile ranges and 43.4% of mammal ranges.

That covers the wildlife trade, traditional medicine, animals caught in fishing gear and animals killed on purpose.

In an interview with Earth.com, Brabant noted that dams, farmland, and farm pollution are widespread, but their weight changes from region to region and group to group.

“This means there is no one-size-fits-all approach to freshwater conservation,” he stated.

The raw material was the Red List kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records for each assessed species the threats experts have seen affecting it.

The team took five groups that have been assessed in full: amphibians, fish, mammals, reptiles, and the dragonflies and damselflies.

For each species, they combined its range map with its threat list.

“By combining this data, we could calculate, for any sub-watershed, the probability that a species occurring there is affected by a particular threat,” Brabant said.

One map per threat per group made 225 maps, which the team stacked into a single index of combined pressure.

Species with small ranges were given more weight.

A threat recorded for a species found in one lake can be placed on the map with confidence, while one recorded for a species spread across a continent can’t.

To test whether the maps mean anything for survival, the team compared them with two separate records.

In the 5% of river basins where extinction risk is modeled to be highest, 71% of the 45 threats were more likely to affect a species than their global average.

The second record was the Living Planet Index, which tracks counts of individual animal populations over time.

Across 2,568 freshwater vertebrate populations from 600 species, populations were shrinking faster in basins with a heavier combined threat load.

Neither record was used to build the maps, so the match is not circular.

The authors wrote that it suggests the maps capture where threats are already pushing freshwater species toward decline.

The study also lined up the freshwater maps against earlier ones made the same way for land vertebrates.

For all seven threats that had been mapped on land, freshwater mammals were more likely to be affected than land mammals.

Freshwater reptiles showed the same pattern with a smaller gap, which the authors put down to the time reptiles still spend on land.

It has been revealed that the hot spots were in different places, too. Where freshwater fish and frogs are under the most pressure is not where land vertebrates are.

“What surprised me most was how different the geography was,” Brabant told Earth.com. Conservation planning has often relied on information about land species, he said.

That is why freshwater species and their threats need to be written into prepares explicitly if the plans are going to reach them.

The Red List treats each threat as if it acted alone, and the authors wrote that many of them combine in ways that could make the damage worse.

In a recent development, the maps estimate how likely species are to be affected in each area. They don’t measure how much harm each threat causes.

Range maps describe where species live today, so places a threat has already emptied may not show up.

Asked which places he would look at first, Brabant said threat alone isn’t enough. Europe and northwestern Africa lead on accumulated threats, while many tropical regions stand out for the number of species affected.

“Areas of high richness and high threat suggest that threat mitigation is most urgent, whereas areas of high richness and low threats would be most suitable for proactive protection,” he noted.

In a recent development, what would help most right now, he mentioned, is reducing the pressures: cleaner water, protected habitat and rivers reconnected. But the most useful action depends on the place and the species.

The next step is matching each basin’s threats to the conservation actions that address them, which the maps alone can’t do yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.
  • The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to concern subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to concern subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

It has been revealed that the letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter notes.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

Industry observers note that “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”.

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself remarked that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

In a recent development, he also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

Industry observers note that and Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

Recent findings suggest that the finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

Industry observers note that “What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi indicates. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

Eksi now prepares to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

In a recent development, “This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi notes. “It’s growing so promptly, the field itself.”.

#88636. What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3233 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the lithium that gave it away, states Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
  • Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, states Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium highlighted they were too late.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data demonstrated way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

It has been revealed that “That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy notes. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

Recent findings suggest that the data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

In a recent development, the number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Industry observers note that since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

Researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a major risk to the space industry, claims Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Sources indicate that six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

“Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” claims José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

Sources indicate that as a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” indicates Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

According to recent reports, spaceX launched its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX looks to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

Recent findings suggest that for decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

Operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he states, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

According to recent reports, aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

In a recent development, injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering looks. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

Industry observers note that “The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy indicates. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

One reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” indicates Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that but in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” notes Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

Recent findings suggest that to quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are currently held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross claims. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

Industry observers note that to do better, scientists are developing new models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

In a recent development, but state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

Sources indicate that to validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens notes. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.

Since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens says.

But in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — launched in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

“We could get close,” Lemmens claims. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens says. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

In a recent development, on Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

The team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

It has been revealed that altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency intends to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” says Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens says.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

Industry observers note that if research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” indicates Ross.

Sources indicate that after scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

Still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he notes.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

Some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, remarked at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

“I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur noted, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks currently available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

Of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, stated at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

Satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, introduced to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

Recent findings suggest that ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he says, “but we just need the resources.”.

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” mentioned Young.

A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that currently defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell states.

In a recent development, can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

In a recent development, kate Wheeling is a freelance journalist based in Santa Barbara, California. She writes about the environment and humans’ relationship with the natural world. Her work has appeared in The Atlantic, Smithsonian magazine, The Daily Beast, and Mother Jones.

#88635. Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1111 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.
  • The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.
  • Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.

The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.

Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.

A new computer simulation called Lumina tracks how gas, dark matter and light interacted through both changes.

It models a region that would span about 1.6 billion light-years on each side at today’s cosmic scale, giving astronomers a way to test their predictions against observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Oliver Zier, a fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, led the project.

Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas was a co-author, along with colleagues at MIT, York University and the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics.

According to recent reports, “With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” Zier said. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions.”.

A simulation is that translation. Astronomers feed in the laws of physics and the universe’s starting conditions, then let a supercomputer calculate how everything develops over time.

In a recent development, they compare the result with real telescope images. A match gives astronomers more confidence in the model. A mismatch can show where its assumptions need more testing.

Lumina covers roughly the first 2 billion years, following the earliest galaxies and the thin gas between them.

The simulated cube is about 1.6 billion light-years on a side, more than 100 times the volume of comparable simulations.

The team divided its contents into 432 billion pieces of gas and dark matter, and each piece of gas has about 3.6 million times the mass of the Sun.

Galaxies grow where the dark matter gathers, strung along the filaments of the cosmic web.

The team ran Lumina on Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

The simulation used 7,536 graphics accelerators, just over 20% of the machine, and about 600 terabytes of working memory at its peak.

Smith described what that size makes possible.

“For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation,” he stated.

Sources indicate that earlier simulations of this kind, including the Thesan project, stopped before helium began to clear. Lumina’s cube is 144 times the volume of Thesan’s.

Sources indicate that the first stars and galaxies cleared the hydrogen slowly and unevenly. In Lumina, bubbles of cleared gas open around the biggest galaxies first and grow until they merge. Regions far from any galaxy stay foggy longest.

The team divided the simulation into 125 regions and tracked how quickly the hydrogen changed in each one.

Recent findings suggest that in a typical region, nearly all of the hydrogen gas between galaxies had lost its electrons by about 1.1 billion years after the Major Bang. In the slowest regions, that took about 1.3 billion years.

Astronomers see the same late finish in the light of distant quasars, which still highlights absorption by hydrogen gas at that time.

Stars did nearly all of this work. Quasars supplied about 15% of the hydrogen-clearing light near the end.

Industry observers note that clearing helium takes light about four times more energetic than clearing hydrogen, and ordinary stars give off very little of it. Quasars do.

A quasar is a supermassive black hole pulling in gas so fast that the gas shines with intense ultraviolet light.

In Lumina, the brightest quasars began stripping helium of its last electron about 900 million years after the Massive Bang. The process was about halfway complete by 1.5 billion years.

By 2 billion years, the regions where helium still held its last electron accounted for less than 1% of the space Lumina modeled.

The bubbles around quasars grew larger than the hydrogen bubbles that formed around galaxies.

It has been revealed that each clearing also heats the gas. The thin gas between galaxies warms to roughly 18,000°F to 36,000°F (10,000°C to 20,000°C) while the hydrogen clears.

It cools as the universe expands, then warms again when the quasar light reaches it.

Measurements of the helium clearing are scarce. Most studies of it rely on fewer than about 25 quasars with a usable line of sight, and Lumina’s timing agrees with those measurements.

According to recent reports, lumina also grows galaxies, and here it fails a test. At about 1.2 billion years after the Massive Bang and earlier, the simulation produces fewer very massive galaxies than Webb has found.

The shortfall grows the further back in time the comparison goes.

The team wrote that this confirms a known problem: galaxy models tuned to the nearby universe undercount the giants Webb sees in the early one.

Stars might form more efficiently in the earliest big galaxies, or the masses astronomers read off Webb’s images might be less certain than assumed.

The simulation can’t settle that on its own, but it marks where the standard picture falls short.

Some of Lumina’s agreement with observations is built in.

The authors set the share of each galaxy’s hydrogen-clearing light that escapes into space at 18%, a value chosen so that hydrogen clears on a realistic schedule. So the timing of that clearing is partly a tuning choice, not a prediction.

The team also slowed the speed of light in the calculation to a fifth of its real value, because the full speed would have made the run unaffordable.

In a recent development, that shortcut may keep hydrogen fog in remote voids a little too long. And the detailed comparison with real quasar spectra, the one that would say whether the helium timing is right, is still to come.

In a recent development, zier’s team intends to release the full Lumina data in 2028. Companion studies are already using it to work out how patchy clearing marks the afterglow of the Big Bang, and how many quasars of each brightness the early universe held.

Observations from Webb and future surveys by the Roman Space Telescope will help astronomers test whether Lumina can explain how the earliest massive galaxies formed.

The full study was published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

#88631. The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2053 w)

The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • In a recent development, in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M.
  • Industry observers note that why are these called the Kids?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

In a recent development, in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

Industry observers note that why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

Recent findings suggest that mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Recent findings suggest that pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — currently larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

Sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

Sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

Zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

Industry observers note that monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

According to recent reports, if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full.

It has been revealed that tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

It has been revealed that A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed promptly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

In a recent development, wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

According to recent reports, the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

In a recent development, sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

Thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

In a recent development, by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

It has been revealed that friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

Sources indicate that you’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

While you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#88629. The wildlife trade is bigger than previously thought, with nearly 80,000 species and counting

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1361 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The wildlife trade is bigger than previously thought, with nearly 80,000 species and counting

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new review finds that global wildlife trade reaches far beyond familiar pets and seafood, and gaps in recordkeeping make its full scale hard to measure.
  • Recent findings suggest that ask about the wildlife trade and most people picture smuggled ivory, tiger skins and pangolins.
  • Most documented wildlife trade is legal, and it includes the fish in the freezer aisle, the orchid on the windowsill, and the gecko in the pet shop window.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new review finds that global wildlife trade reaches far beyond familiar pets and seafood, and gaps in recordkeeping make its full scale hard to measure.

Recent findings suggest that ask about the wildlife trade and most people picture smuggled ivory, tiger skins and pangolins. Almost none of the recorded trade is like that.

Most documented wildlife trade is legal, and it includes the fish in the freezer aisle, the orchid on the windowsill, and the gecko in the pet shop window.

A new review documented 79,554 species in international wildlife trade, well above the roughly 50,000 previously estimated.

A broader tally that included species people use for subsistence and other purposes reached 107,356.

Even the latest number is likely a considerable underestimate, the authors wrote, because almost no country records what it buys and sells.

Sources indicate that alice Hughes, a conservation scientist at the University of Melbourne, led the review. Her co-authors come from the organizations that track wildlife trade, including TRAFFIC, the IUCN and the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization.

The count comes from stitching together databases built for other purposes, and the plant half of it rests on records of use rather than records of sale.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hughes said the finding is about ordinary buyers as much as smugglers.

“Almost all of us are part of wildlife trade, and whilst some of that, such as fisheries are managed, sectors like the pet trade are not,” she said.

Legal wildlife trade is worth an estimated $220 billion to $300 billion a year. Smuggled wildlife is worth an estimated $28 billion to $40 billion.

So the legal side is roughly six to 11 times larger than the smuggling that gets the attention.

“When we think of wildlife trade we tend to think about the illegal trade of elephants, tigers and pangolins. But it’s much more than that,” Hughes said.

“Wildlife trade includes everything from timber, seafood and medicinal plants to pets, cut flowers, ornamental fish and fungi, and most of it is legal.”.

Legal doesn’t mean harmless. Where researchers have population numbers for a traded species, the populations being collected from are, on average, 50% to 60% smaller than populations left alone.

By one estimate the authors cite, trade has contributed, directly or indirectly, to the global extinction of 294 species.

It has been revealed that the team pulled together every trade record it could reach. The largest was the CITES Trade Database, which holds the records of legal trade in protected species going back to 1975.

Alongside it went the IUCN Red List, UN fish and timber records, TRAFFIC’s seizure reports and the US import database.

Beyond the databases, the researchers drew on published surveys of individual animal groups and a world checklist of plants that people use.

Animals accounted for 47,685 species, and up to 31,306 of those are vertebrates. That works out to 42% of every vertebrate species science has described.

Put another way, two out of every five kinds of animal with a backbone have been traded somewhere.

It has been revealed that for birds, the share is higher still: about 65% of all living bird species have been traded. Plants and fungi added 59,671 species potentially used or traded.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service logs wild animal shipments into and out of the United States in a database called LEMIS, and it periodically releases the records.

Since 2000, more than 21,000 wild animal species have been traded into the US alone.

In a recent development, more than a quarter of all traded animal species appear in that one country’s records and in no other database. For mammals, the figure is 54%.

Much of what the world knows about which animals are traded comes from one country’s import records.

Hughes’s team surveyed 61 countries and searched for “wildlife trade database” in 30 languages. The US system was the only full, public record of trade across groups of animals from any country.

“The United States is the only country that systematically records and publicly shares trade data across a wide range of taxa. For much of the rest of the world, equivalent data simply does not exist,” Hughes said.

Asked what it would take for other countries to follow, Hughes told Earth.com it starts with accepting that “legal trade is not necessarily sustainable.”.

Without data on trade in other groups, she mentioned, the trade can’t be managed to make sure it is sustainable.

“Trade has changed, the exotic pet trade will continue to grow, and with so many species in trade, that poses a real risk unless we start monitoring it better,” she remarked.

The pet trade is where the upcoming counts diverge most from the old global estimates. The gaps are largest for reptiles, invertebrates and plants, which are also the hardest to track.

A lizard or a beetle bought online travels by mail and often isn’t identified to species at the border.

CITES, the treaty that regulates trade in at-risk species, covers about 9.5% of reptile species. The new review recorded 4,620 reptile species in trade, about 37% of all described reptiles.

Asked which traded species surprised her most, Hughes remarked it was how quickly newly described species appear for sale.

Collectors sometimes use the scientific descriptions themselves to find animals to trade, she stated. She also pointed to “the price people are willing to pay for some, like 100s of dollars for a single isopod (woodlouse).”.

For buyers, Hughes said the place to start is where an animal came from.

Corn snakes and leopard geckos should be captive bred, she remarked, and chameleons often come from the wild and don’t survive well in captivity.

“If you are not sure where they come from, just don’t buy them, for every wild caught animal in the shop, many others die in transit,” she remarked.

Governments have agreed on a set of global biodiversity targets, and one of them covers the impacts of trade.

Its single headline measure is the share of fish stocks being fished at sustainable levels. By the review’s count, that measure reflects about 2% of the species in use and trade.

“While the global biodiversity framework does have a target on trade, based on our estimates it only accounts for around two or three percent of species in trade and misses the other 97 percent,” Hughes remarked.

The authors wrote that the fix doesn’t need a upcoming system. Almost every country already runs customs checks and animal health checks on imports, and most CITES permits are still paper.

Electronic permits exist, but only about 30 of the 184 CITES countries use them.

If customs offices digitized shipping invoices and matched them to a species list, the authors wrote, they would record much of what is now lost.

The United Kingdom has required an electronic tag on every sheep, and a log of its movements, since 2009, so record-keeping on that scale is already being done.

Recent findings suggest that seizure records reflect how hard a country enforces its laws as much as how much is smuggled. And the databases don’t agree with one another on which species are traded, which is part of the paper’s point.

Even so, Hughes mentioned the estimate is still an underestimate, because most countries do not collect the data.

According to recent reports, the larger question is whether wild populations can sustain the trade. An IUCN working group has assessed the potential sustainability of trade for 347 species across 117 countries.

For many traded species, researchers still lack the data to tell how much is being taken from the wild and how those populations are faring.

Hughes and her co-authors propose standardizing how trade data are collected and starting at a regional level, with the European Union as a possible first model.

Until that happens, each newly introduced database that opens is likely to add species to the count.

For many species, researchers still can’t tell how trade is affecting wild populations.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that as Rep.
  • A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Industry observers note that as Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

It has been revealed that rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie mentioned his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

Sources indicate that “They could be a hero if they sign it,” he remarked, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

Industry observers note that the bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie noted he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The fresh bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Industry observers note that now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the concern in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”.

In a recent development, “Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie stated. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor.".

How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself.
  • “I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.
  • According to recent reports, he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

According to recent reports, he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

Industry observers note that more recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin notes.

The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics
