📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day.
  • Sources indicate that for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

Sources indicate that for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he says he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

It has been revealed that scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

According to recent reports, but it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

Then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first significant clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic indicates. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

In a recent development, masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

Industry observers note that the research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic says. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

It has been revealed that originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

In a recent development, while lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

The team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

In a recent development, roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less fresh material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

Recent findings suggest that our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, says Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

Recent findings suggest that in fact, Masic co-founded a organization in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also looks to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Manasee Wagh contributed to this story.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 19: Mercury moves into Libra.

The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

Industry observers note that from Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Florida’s invasive pythons don’t always stay on the ground, and about 1 in 7 adult sightings were up in trees

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A USGS study found that invasive Burmese pythons in Florida sometimes climb trees, especially in winter, raising concerns for nesting birds.
  • Burmese pythons invading southern Florida are not primarily tree-dwellers, but some of them climb.
  • For 168 juveniles, the share was about 17 percent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A USGS study found that invasive Burmese pythons in Florida sometimes climb trees, especially in winter, raising concerns for nesting birds.

Burmese pythons invading southern Florida are not primarily tree-dwellers, but some of them climb. Among 188 radio-tracked adults, about 14 percent, or roughly 1 in 7, were found in a tree or shrub at least once, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

For 168 juveniles, the share was about 17 percent. Across more than 4,000 observations, however, fewer than 3 percent placed a python in a tree or shrub.

Both age groups were most likely to climb in December and January, the cooler months of southern Florida’s dry season.

Each observation came from locating a snake through radio telemetry, not from a chance sighting. Tracking ran from November 2017 to December 2024 in Big Cypress National Preserve.

Lisa McBride, a biologist at the USGS Fort Collins Science Center, is the study’s first author.

A public USGS data release lists 112 tracking events in trees or shrubs, involving 56 different pythons.

It has been revealed that the first python was observed in the Everglades in 1979, but no more were seen until 1995. The species now breeds in the preserve and is spreading through south Florida.

Burmese pythons, one of Florida’s invasive reptiles, are notoriously difficult to find. By some estimates, the probability of detecting an individual python can be less than 5 percent.

Adults in trees were seen basking, resting, brooding eggs or gathering with other pythons. Juveniles rested, basked or moved between tree limbs.

Most adults found in trees during the peak climbing months were basking, a behavior that lets reptiles absorb heat from their surroundings.

The researchers suggest pythons may use trees and shrubs at that time of year to maintain a high body temperature.

According to recent reports, in February 2022, one adult male basked atop a Brazilian peppertree about 16 feet (5 meters) above the ground. It then climbed to the crown of a cabbage palm, about 23 feet (7 meters) up.

A female brooded her eggs in a fallen, hollow cypress tree about 6.5 feet (2 meters) above the ground in May 2022.

A juvenile female rested on a pond apple tree about 5 feet (1.5 meters) up that same May.

A USGS video reveals a juvenile female moving across the branches of a dahoon holly tree in the preserve.

The higher share among juveniles may reflect an ontogenetic shift, a change in habitat use as an animal grows, the researchers suggest.

The probability of finding a python in a tree generally fell as its weight rose. Smaller snakes may move through branches more easily than heavy adults.

Still, trees with strong branches, such as Brazilian peppertrees and live oaks, supported some of the largest pythons tracked.

In a recent development, adults caught in Florida average 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The species can reach 19 feet (5.8 meters), however.

Native from India to lower China, the Malay Peninsula and some islands of the East Indies, Burmese pythons are semi-aquatic and excellent climbers.

The exact route of their introduction is unknown. Pythons likely escaped from a breeding facility destroyed during Hurricane Andrew, and pet pythons have likely been released in and around the Everglades.

Industry observers note that the months when adult pythons were most likely to be in trees overlap with the nesting season of several wading-bird species. Earlier studies documented pythons preying on nests of great egrets and white ibises in the Everglades.

No python was seen preying on birds in trees during the tracking. The USGS cautioned that the overlap does not mean tree use is causing bird declines.

Rather, it identifies another behavior that could bring an invasive predator into contact with vulnerable animals, and an area for continued research.

More than 25 percent of captured pythons have birds in their stomachs.

In a recent development, before 2000, mammals were encountered frequently during nocturnal road surveys in Everglades National Park. Road surveys from 2003 to 2011 then recorded a 99.3 percent drop in raccoon observations as pythons spread.

Sources indicate that opossum observations fell by 98.9 percent and bobcat observations by 87.5 percent. The same surveys failed to detect rabbits.

Some reports put the south Florida python population anywhere from 5,000 to 180,000 snakes, though the best estimates so far place it closer to 30,000.

Almost 28,000 wild Burmese pythons have been removed from Florida’s environment and reported to the FWC since 2000. The 2026 Florida Python Challenge alone removed 280, with 907 participants from 30 U.S. states, Canada and Vietnam.

It has been revealed that the South Florida Water Management District also pays agents an hourly rate to hunt pythons. They earn $50 for each snake up to 4 feet (1.2 meters), $25 for each additional foot (0.3 meters) and $200 for each verified active nest.

Seasonal data on tree use “could improve the effectiveness of removal efforts by management agencies,” the authors wrote.

Knowing when pythons climb could also help scientists understand how the snakes interact with the Greater Everglades ecosystem.

The study was published in the journal Journal of Herpetology.

Dan Bartlett from June Lake, California.

Asteroid 6993 (1995 BJ4), a small body 7 miles (11 kilometers) across, orbits in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. In August 2026, astronomers spotted a faint tail, making it candidate for the largest known main-belt comet. However, the tail has been gradually fading through 2026, which hints at it being caused by debris from a one-time impact rather than ongoing outgassing, astronomers reported last month in a paper accepted in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. In this image, the tail spans more than 35′, or wider than the Full Moon.

4.6 hours of exposure with two 11-inch f/2.2 Celestron RASA telescopes, ZWO ASI6200MM Pro (monochrome) and ZWO ASI6200MC Pro (one-shot color) cameras.

  • The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul presently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he looks to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul presently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

Industry observers note that the move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul mentioned in a press release that he aims to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”.

Recent findings suggest that he cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote.

Paul, an ophthalmologist, noted at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Recent findings suggest that lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he mentioned, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”.

Recent findings suggest that but he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”.

Industry observers note that lankford stated he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”.

Breaking: A dinosaur found by a Montana rancher on her land in 2019 sold for $47.3 million, over five times its top estimate

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in Latest York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million.
  • Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in Latest York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million. Its pre-sale estimate was $6 million to $9 million.

Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.

Six bidders competed for more than 12 minutes, the auction house said. Jodi is now the second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction.

The record belongs to “Gus,” a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton that sold at Sotheby’s New York for $50.1 million on July 14, 2026.

According to recent reports, according to Guinness World Records, Gus broke the record set by “Apex,” a Stegosaurus also sold at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York. Apex fetched $44.6 million on July 17, 2024.

Industry observers note that sotheby’s reports its results including the buyer’s premium, the fee added to the winning bid. The hammer price for Jodi has not been made public.

Jodi was the only lot in its own dedicated sale. Neither the buyer nor the seller has been named.

Its listed provenance is a private collection that acquired the skeleton in 2021.

Sotheby’s lists Jodi as Nanotyrannus cf. lancensis, from the Hell Creek Formation, about 67 million years old. The abbreviation “cf.” marks a provisional identification.

A crew of seven, including Pierson and Clayton Phipps, dug up the skeleton in a single field season. It comprises about 191 fossil bone elements from one individual.

It has been revealed that its virtually complete skull has 53 bones and roughly 50 teeth. The rarely preserved wishbone is intact, and about half of the belly ribs, or gastralia, survived.

Missing parts were restored with 3D-printed and sculpted elements, and the mounted skeleton measures about 19.6 feet (6 meters) from nose to tail. It stands about 9 feet 6 inches (2.9 meters) tall, not 6 feet 5 inches (2 meters) as first listed.

Recent findings suggest that the auction house describes the animal as an adult, based on its overall size and degree of bone development. It cites no peer-reviewed study of the skeleton.

According to recent reports, at the Frieze Masters art fair in 2023, the same skeleton was exhibited as a juvenile T. rex.

For decades, many paleontologists argued that Nanotyrannus fossils were simply young T. rex. The debate centered on a skull collected in Montana in 1942 by the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

In a recent development, in 1988, a team that included museum curator Dr. Michael Williams named it Nanotyrannus lancensis. In December 2025, a study in Science found that the skull’s throat bone had stopped growing, indicating a mature animal.

It has been revealed that in October 2025, a study in Nature concluded that the tyrannosaur in the “Dueling Dinosaurs” fossil was a fully grown Nanotyrannus lancensis. Growth rings and fused vertebrae put its age at about 20 years.

It has been revealed that that animal had larger forelimbs, more teeth and fewer tail vertebrae than T. rex, the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences reported.

After examining more than 200 tyrannosaur fossils, the researchers also named a second species, Nanotyrannus lethaeus, after the River Lethe of Greek mythology.

Sources indicate that “This fossil doesn’t just settle the debate. It flips decades of T. rex research on its head,” Lindsay Zanno, head of paleontology at the North Carolina museum and a co-author of the study, noted in 2025.

Before the Gus auction, the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology issued a statement on scientifically significant fossils. It called for them to be permanently curated in accredited museums, universities and other public research institutions.

Sources indicate that without provisions for long-term access, private ownership may permanently diminish opportunities for future research, education and public engagement, the society warned. It also recognized the important role of private landowners, amateur fossil enthusiasts and commercial excavators.

“The discovery of an important fossil is only the beginning of its scientific story,” said Kristina Curry Rogers, the society’s vice president at the time.

In a recent development, “Many of the most significant advances in paleontology have come years or even decades after a fossil was collected,” she noted. Fresh analytical methods and technologies allowed scientists to ask entirely new questions of specimens already housed in museums.

According to recent reports, after the Jodi sale, Curry Rogers and Zanno published an opinion piece on fossil auctions. They wrote that they hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education.

Under Montana law, fossils are part of the surface estate, so they normally belong to whoever owns the land.

It has been revealed that the provision, enacted in 2019, claims the word “minerals” does not include fossils unless a deed or other instrument clearly states otherwise. A landowner can sever fossil rights from the land through a clear and express grant.

Sotheby’s offered Jodi with full rights and documentation certifying its condition, authenticity and the legality of its ownership.

The federal Paleontological Resources Preservation Act of 2009 does not apply to state, private or Indian lands, according to the Bureau of Land Management.

The information was obtained from Sotheby’s.

The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Massive Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

📅 07 Nov 2018 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator.
  • The term “home generator” can be confusing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

Recent findings suggest that there are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

According to recent reports, the DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a substantial boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

It has been revealed that the generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display highlights you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden.

It has been revealed that technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Recent findings suggest that its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

In a recent development, with three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support highlighted its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an problem with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Sources indicate that ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

According to recent reports, you can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review.

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

It has been revealed that several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

Industry observers note that while it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

Industry observers note that there are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (key for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

According to recent reports, it’s vital to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That noted, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Sources indicate that once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

Recent findings suggest that the two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review.

Recent findings suggest that battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

Recent findings suggest that the power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

Sources indicate that during testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Industry observers note that pulsar is a relatively latest brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator highlighted up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

Sources indicate that the generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

In a recent development, we have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

According to recent reports, you could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.).

It has been revealed that in addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

Sources indicate that the two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

Sources indicate that if you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, plan on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

Recent findings suggest that A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

In a recent development, it’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Recent findings suggest that different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other challenges in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

Sources indicate that so why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

It has been revealed that but because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Sources indicate that standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

When you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

It has been revealed that my generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll enhancement this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

It has been revealed that the 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The phases of the Moon are: Latest Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

RELATED: 20 things to see on the Moon.

In a recent development, there are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

It has been revealed that super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a Upcoming Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

Recent findings suggest that how does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and Upcoming Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Industry observers note that democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

It has been revealed that colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

In a recent development, “I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

Sources indicate that with his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

According to recent reports, republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

In a recent development, colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

It has been revealed that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer noted last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I noted, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Recent findings suggest that still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Recent findings suggest that colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” notes a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

According to recent reports, the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Sources indicate that grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” claims Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

It has been revealed that moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

According to recent reports, “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz states. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The only thing worse than discovering your car has a dead battery is having it happen when it’s raining. If you live in a wet environment as I do in Oregon, you’ll be glad you own a portable jump starter like the Noco Boost Plus GB40. With its three watertight ports closed, it’s impervious to dust intrusion—but more importantly, its IP65 rating means it can withstand heavy rain and even low-pressure blasts with a hose.

Sources indicate that besides its consummate performance in wet conditions, the GB40 is worth considering because it’s compact, lightweight (just over 2 pounds), and relatively easy to use. I also appreciate that it includes spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection, an output port for charging portable electronics, and a six-mode flashlight.

That said, the GB40 isn’t perfect. While I found that it punched above its weight in jump-starting power and its battery life is adequate, it isn’t the most powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve recently tested, and its 2,150 milliampere-hour (mAh) capacity is definitely on the lower side. It also doesn’t have an LED screen but rather uses lights as indicators of its status and operation. Even more crucially, it uses a manual override function to boost severely depleted batteries instead of a dedicated boost button.

I tested the Noco Boost Plus GB40 over several months in Oregon spanning the wet and dry seasons. When testing a portable jump starter, I evaluate how rapidly it starts a vehicle, how many jump-starts it provides before needing to be recharged, how easy it is to use, its features, and the number and effectiveness of its auxiliary power ports to charge portable devices such as a smartphone.

It has been revealed that the Noco GB40 easily fits in the palm of my hand, and the rubberized case and ribs built into each side make it easy to grip, which is important when working around an engine with moving parts. Its small size also means it’s easier to store in a vehicle’s glove box than a larger device like the Gooloo GT6000, which I recommend as the best portable jump starter for most people.

Recent findings suggest that the Noco GB40 doesn’t have an LED screen like many of the portable jump starters from Gooloo, its main competitor. But the touch-based control panel on one side makes it relatively simple to operate. This consists of a large power button with a white on/off LED next to it, a four-segment multicolor battery-level indicator that reveals the state of charge in 25 percent increments, an error indicator, a boost LED, a manual override button, and a button for the flashlight.

Sources indicate that with a peak output of only 1,000 amps, the Noco Boost Plus GB40 is the least powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve tested. Its 2,150 mAh rating also makes it the lowest in reserve-power capacity. That said, it had no concerns jump-starting my Honda Element when I left the lights on and drained the battery. It even cranked the 6.8-liter V10 in my RV when I came back to it after months in storage and found the battery depleted.

I also intentionally left it powered on (since it doesn’t have an automatic shutoff like the Astro AI S8, which I recommend for its value) and it lasted about 24 hours before shutting down. Via a 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-C input, it charges about as fast as other portable jump starters with the same specs, and it took just under four hours to charge from 0 to 100 percent using the supplied USB-C cable.

In a recent development, among features, the flashlight on the GB40 is the most compelling. It has six modes, including an SOS and strobe, which puts it well ahead of the competition. It also has two lenses, one on each side of the output ports, whereas most portable jump starters use a single flashlight lens. While the flashlight isn’t as bright as some others at 100 lumens (for comparison, the $70 Gooloo GP2000, has a 400-lumen flashlight), I found the Noco GB40 more than adequate for use at night.

Industry observers note that the Noco GB40’s USB-C charging input doesn’t double as an output port to charge portable devices, which puts it at a disadvantage. It has just one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging portable electronics (the Gooloo GP2000 has two) and charged my iPhone 16 from 0 percent to 80 percent in about two hours.

Instead of a boost button that supplies a bit more amperage to jump-start a very dead battery, the GB40 has a manual override button that, when pushed and held for three seconds, detects a severely depleted battery (below three volts).

Recent findings suggest that it’s a far less user-friendly feature, plus it disables the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection. As such, users need to be extra careful not to allow the cable clamps to touch, which can cause dangerous sparking. To complicate things further, the GB40 has an LED labeled “boost” that’s simply an indicator light to let you know the device is properly connected to the battery.

In a recent development, there are certainly much more powerful portable jump starters than the Noco Boost Plus GB40 and much of the competition offers features that are far more convenient (albeit for a higher price point), perhaps most significantly, a boost button. Above all, the GB40’s waterproof rating is the best reason to buy it, plus its compact size, six-mode flashlight, and emergency charging for small devices make it an appealing choice. It also provides ample and reliable power to give a dead battery in most vehicles a boost and start the engine.

Other Portable Jump Starters We Recommend.

The Gooloo GT6000 packs 27,000 mAh of reserve power capacity and 6,000-amp peak current. This allows it to jump-start vehicles ranging from a small motorcycle to a heavy-duty truck with a 12.0-liter diesel engine. The GT6000 offers a standby time of two years, and it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after just seven minutes of recharging. It’s got a heap of charging ports, including a 100-watt USB-C in/out that can top off the internal battery from empty to full in 1.4 hours. The device’s 3.2-inch screen makes checking battery level, charging output, and more easy and foolproof.

Recent findings suggest that with 4,000 amps of peak current and 24,000 mAh of capacity, the Wolfbox can jump-start up to 10.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines. It holds a charge for more than a year. The 1.5-cubic-foot-per-minute air pump takes one minute to inflate a 17-inch tire from 30 to 36 psi. It also has a 65-watt USB-C in/out port to promptly recharge the internal battery, two USB-A ports to charge other devices, and a 400-lumen, three-mode LED flashlight.

The Noco AX65 combines a portable jump starter and a portable air compressor into a single device. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power. The tire inflator pumps out 2.3 cubic feet per minute of airflow. The jump starter cranks gas engines up to 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. The tire inflator has a digital display, auto shutoff, and memory settings like other air compressors I’ve tested but also pauses and then resumes inflation when a set pressure is reached to ensure proper inflation.

  • Richard Talcott is a former senior editor and current contributing editor of Astronomy.

After more than 20 years of planning, construction, and testing, astronomers have officially started the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). The survey will snap about 1,000 images per night with a 3.2-gigapixel camera — the largest digital camera in the world — attached to the 8.4-meter telescope at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile. The LSST will observe the entire southern sky every three to four nights, on average, across its 10-year lifetime. The goal: build a high-definition, time-lapse record of the cosmos from the solar system to distant galaxies. This part of the initial image covers about 1.7° by 1.7° centered in northeastern Centaurus, though the left side bleeds into Lupus. The wispy swirls are tenuous clouds of gas and dust known as galactic cirrus, illuminated by the diffuse glow of the Milky Way.

Richard Talcott is a former senior editor and current contributing editor of Astronomy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

Sources indicate that “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer notes. “You have to really be curious.”.

Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

Recent findings suggest that in September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer notes it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

According to recent reports, minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

Sources indicate that “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.
