  • Eicher is one of the most widely recognized astronomy enthusiasts in the world.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 20, 1889, Edwin Hubble was born in Marshfield, Missouri. His 1923 observations of the Andromeda Galaxy and a Cepheid variable within it would vastly expand our understanding of other galaxies and the size of the universe. (See Oct. 5th, 1923: Hubble discovers galaxies beyond the Milky Way.).

In addition to that monumental discovery, Hubble also developed a system for sorting galaxies: In the 1930s, Hubble began to study and classify galaxies into their various so-called morphological types, the array of structures astronomers saw in photographs. He eventually assembled the types of galaxies he observed into a tuning fork-shaped diagram. It contained spiral galaxies, barred spiral galaxies — spirals containing a linear “bar” of material passing through their centers — lenticular (lens-shaped) galaxies, and elliptical galaxies. He also identified irregular galaxies, clouds of stars and gas that lacked an organized shape. Later on, astronomers identified peculiar galaxies, systems that appeared to be wracked with explosive or disruptive events. They also identified a class of galaxies called dwarf spheroidals, which seemed to be numerous in the local universe.

It has been revealed that david J. Eicher is one of the most widely recognized astronomy enthusiasts in the world. He has been with Astronomy magazine since 1982, beginning as an assistant editor and working through associate, senior, and managing positions. He was editor in chief from 2002 to 2025 and is at the moment the magazine’s Editor Emeritus.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 20: The Moon passes Saturn and Neptune.

If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

According to recent reports, located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — currently larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

If you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any latest bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

Recent findings suggest that the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., noted in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

Recent findings suggest that “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At concern in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura noted his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He stated that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He stated the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors remarked he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A upcoming Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Industry observers note that congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco stated he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

Sources indicate that the House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a upcoming version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

Nov. 21, 1993: The death of Bruno Rossi

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (213 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in Venice, Italy, in 1905, Bruno Rossi attended the University of Bologna, graduating with a doctorate in physics in 1927.
  • Throughout his long career across countries and institutions, Rossi laid the groundwork for the study of several key fields in astronomy and astrophysics.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Born in Venice, Italy, in 1905, Bruno Rossi attended the University of Bologna, graduating with a doctorate in physics in 1927. When race-based laws inspired by his country’s growing closeness with Nazi Germany meant the Jewish Rossi had to leave Italy, he made his way to the U.S. In 1940, Rossi became an associate professor of physics at Cornell University, and from 1943-1946, he worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos Laboratory. After the war, Rossi joined the faculty of MIT, where he remained until his retirement in the early ’70s.

Throughout his long career across countries and institutions, Rossi laid the groundwork for the study of several key fields in astronomy and astrophysics. His research into cosmic rays became the basis of high-energy particle physics, while his pioneering search for cosmic X-rays jump-started X-ray astronomy. Rossi also conducted trailblazing research into the interplanetary medium, and contributed to the development of public policy for space exploration. Rossi passed away at age 88 on Nov. 21, 1993. Today, among other honors and memorials that Rossi accrued, the Bruno B. Rossi Prize for astrophysics is awarded yearly.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence.
  • To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models.
  • Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust.

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

Sources indicate that in the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo claims. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

Industry News: The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created.
  • The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot newly introduced multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive fresh display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot newly introduced multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

My evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV shows via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

Sources indicate that I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best upcoming mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

Sources indicate that RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot new display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

When TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive new mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

It has been revealed that SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

The newly introduced display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

Sources indicate that the TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

Industry observers note that one sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

It has been revealed that the step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

The QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

Recent findings suggest that the TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

Recent findings suggest that hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

According to recent reports, under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker reveals in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor issue. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

It has been revealed that after skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

Sources indicate that the UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

It has been revealed that hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an update for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its new mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

It has been revealed that maybe just as impressive are the issues the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a big surprise.

According to recent reports, when it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A big reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That noted, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance complications, so it’s important to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

It has been revealed that all of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of latest content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

Sources indicate that as for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

All of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

Recent findings suggest that in contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other new technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

The most notable connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

WiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

All the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s notable to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

It has been revealed that each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is important for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

It has been revealed that if you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

#88593. 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

📅 31 Oct 2025 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3303 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theplanetd ↗ Open Full Page

21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

📅 31 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December.
  • But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa.
  • In a recent development, in fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In a recent development, in fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

According to recent reports, we once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

Sources indicate that we were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

Recent findings suggest that if your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

Industry observers note that we thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

According to recent reports, sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like Newly introduced York City at Christmas.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

We’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Recent findings suggest that where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

It has been revealed that we love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

Sources indicate that we’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A Newly introduced Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Industry observers note that why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

In a recent development, we went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks demonstrates are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Recent findings suggest that visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

It has been revealed that here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

We’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Industry observers note that jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

According to recent reports, this was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

For the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

In a recent development, yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

December is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

Sources indicate that we hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you proposal your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

#88592. Tech Report: Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

Tech Report: Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Sources indicate that think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go.
  • Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, says Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Sources indicate that think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, says Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Industry observers note that well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

“Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys states. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

Sources indicate that first, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

Since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

And the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

It has been revealed that your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea says. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

According to recent reports, overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

“It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys says. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more important at that point in time.”.

This 9-Year-Old Owns Dozens of Vintage Toilets. He May Have Found His Calling in Plumbing—and Is Inspiring Others.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • It has been revealed that like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube.
  • Now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

It has been revealed that like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube. Unlike most kids his age, Damian also loves toilets, a passion he discovered on the social media platform.

Now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank. Standing on the 11-toilet, fully plumbed platform his dad built in the family’s Eastern Washington backyard, Damian points out their trapways, the fill valves, the siphon jets, the lid bolts, and, of course, the pièce de resistance—the flush.

It has been revealed that roger Skaer, Damian’s dad, claims his son’s obsession began a few years ago. “He stumbled across these plumbers on YouTube who replace toilets, test them, fix them, and, man, he just loves watching videos of people working on toilets,” Roger says. “There’s been a lot of engineering behind toilet evolution over the last 100 years, and he’s fascinated by it.”.

Recent findings suggest that damian’s collection began when he found a couple of old toilets in his grandparents’ barn. Since then, he has amassed about 40, according to Roger. Each week, new models arrive from brands looking to collaborate with the 9-year-old.

In a recent development, while the topic of young people and screens continues to cause serious consternation among adults, for some kids, they’re serving as an introduction to the skilled trades, occupations like carpentry, welding, and plumbing that have struggled to attract and retain newly introduced talent. According to a 2026 National Association of House Builders survey, only 6 percent of young adults 18 to 25 planned to pursue a career in construction trades.

It has been revealed that but a crop of young social media influencers are bucking that trend. Guiseppe D’Anna has been working on cars at his dad’s collision repair shop since he was six; today Guiseppe’s Garage has a quarter-million followers on YouTube, and the automotive wunderkind is on “a mission to help shape the next generation of gearheads.” British woodworker Gabriel River Clark has been creating DIY content since he was 12, crafting anything from dinnerware to toys to home decor. On TikTok, 10-year-old Jackson Laux, a.k.a. Just a Jackson Thing, delights his roughly million followers with his deep knowledge of vintage tractors and mowers.

This kind of early exposure is vital to promoting trade occupations, claims Paul Goodrum, PhD, a professor in Construction Engineering and Management at the University of Colorado Boulder. While lots of kids used to learn these skills in high school shop or career tech classes, over the past few decades, policy makers and administrators have phased vocational educational courses out of high school curriculums, emphasizing core academic subjects and college readiness instead. The best vocational programs, according to Goodrum, tend to exist in alternative schools for students with behavioral challenges.

“There is a bit of a disconnect between how we measure the quality of our schools and what the economy and the workforce needs in this country,” he states. “As an industry, we really need to be trying to more actively expose kids to these career paths not just in high school but middle school too.”.

But it’s a vicious cycle, Goodrum claims: fewer trades workers mean fewer teachers to teach vocational classes, “and how do you convince someone to give up a really high-paying job to go teach high school?”.

Industry observers note that the shortage of skilled workers is creating headaches for more than just hiring managers. A reduced workforce is causing construction project costs to soar and go over schedule. It’s also turning worksites into danger zones, as understaffed crews are working longer hours at a brutal pace. In 2024, construction workers accounted for about one in five workplace deaths in the country.

Sources indicate that most workers who end up in trade occupations do so later in life, often as a second career. The average age of an apprentice in a construction program is 28, for instance, while plumbing and electrical apprentices are often pushing 40.

Recent findings suggest that “For so long we nurtured this culture saying you’ve got to go to college and get this degree or that degree, and if you end up working in construction it was because you somehow failed,” says Roger Skaer, a trained carpenter. “I think it’s a product of a long-lived, misguided representation of what success should look like.”.

Recently, young people have started to question that college-or-bust narrative. Between 2020 and 2025, enrollment in two-year vocational or trade schools grew by almost 20 percent. And while the trades have their own difficulties—dangerous work conditions, wear and tear on the body—they offer something lots of other fields can’t right now: job security. According to the New Hampshire–based nonprofit Bring Back the Trades, more than 1.4 million trade jobs will be vacant in 2030.

According to recent reports, roger is confident that eventually Damian will fill one of those positions. “Right now, he’s saying plumber, I’m thinking maybe a toilet designer,” he indicates, explaining that Damian’s been angling for a 3D printer so that he can build his own commodes. “I truly feel he's going to be in some kind of trade or hands-on craftwork.”.

And if toilets don’t pan out, Damian has a backup hobby: washer and dryer installation and repair.

#88589. Trump indicates no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (760 w)

Trump indicates no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, president Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day.
  • President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.
  • Recent findings suggest that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, president Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

Recent findings suggest that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Industry observers note that vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

Industry observers note that "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night.".

Trump has noted that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

Industry observers note that “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

Sources indicate that the situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Sources indicate that trump, Vance and other administration officials have remarked in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday indicated that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "rapidly.".

Industry observers note that “Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

Sources indicate that as the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

Recent findings suggest that “With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

According to recent reports, in the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed. For instance, a 2026 National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA) report predicts that cremation will account for more than 64 percent of funerary arrangements this year. Likewise, an NFDA release from 2025 claims that more than 61 percent of consumers are interested in exploring “green funeral” options.

Some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction. It doesn’t require high heat generation, it doesn’t take up space like a traditional burial, and it creates a natural source of plant nutrition. It’s a way to truly return to the earth.

According to recent reports, in a human composting center, workers place a body into a contained ecosystem along with natural bedding like mulch and hay, and periodically tend to each habitat (similar to how you rotate your compost.) The process that Katrina Spade helped to design at her manufacturer—Recompose, based in Seattle—is modeled on one used to compost dead livestock; in testing, she hired a soil scientist to ensure that the heat of the composting process was enough to kill any pathogens. This happens in plant and animal composting, too.

It has been revealed that at a similar company, Return Home, the process digests the soft tissues of the body into nutrients in the soil. Then the bones and any medical devices can be removed, and the latter are recycled. The company uses a cremulator, a traditional cremation tool, to grind bones into pieces. Like a coffee grinder or blender, the cremulator’s rotating blades turn larger pieces into smaller ones. The resulting finer particulate of bone is ideal for composting.

Sources indicate that today, people interested in burial have a lot of choices. That’s partly because strict laws and taboos around burying people outside of cemeteries or other designated places are changing. A majority of states allow burial on private property, some with caveats. Embalming is not required across the board. Even the required depth of burial varies a lot, and some states don’t have a depth requirement.

Recent findings suggest that for some people, allowing unembalmed burial on private land isn’t enough. Many people will never own land in a rural enough place to comfortably bury a loved one. Cemeteries have been running out of space for a while, and experts say fewer people want the traditional American ceremonies linked with death, like viewings and services at funeral homes and churches. But that doesn’t mean people don’t want their death to bring closure, a sense of ritual, or a meaningful return to the earth.

Cities have long had unique challenges with human burial because of their population density. Neighborhoods might eventually surround cemeteries on the edge of town by the time they need to expand. Our parklike modern cemeteries date back to just Victorian times, when they were boosted as part of an overall public park movement in the United Kingdom. Even Brooklyn’s iconic Green-Wood Cemetery started as a public park. But while taxes fund parks, cemeteries are often privately owned. When they stop having open spaces to sell, they start losing income. It grows ethically murky very fast.

This is where human composting enters the scene. As a graduate student, Spade first introduced the idea in her architecture thesis in 2013, The Verge reports. She wondered if people in cities might proposal to send their dead bodies to clean, organized spaces where caretakers could use nature’s own processes to speed up decomposition—or “recomposition,” as she calls it. This results in an amount of enriched soil, because the human body is full of nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphate that plants need.

It works a lot like any other composting system, or wild life cycle, such as a decomposing log or whale fall—when dead whales sink and become an instant food source for other creatures. Natural topsoil called humus hosts organisms whose place in the ecosystem is to digest animal and plant matter into soil. On the spectrum of humus decomposers, earthworms fall on the larger end, while microbes and tiny insects fall on the smaller end. Together, they form a food web, with each organism playing a part, like digesting a particular nutrient or a particular size of particle.

According to recent reports, “Death market” figures show the overall rise in cremation rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cremation results in a small, tangible object that can be buried anytime, without the countdown to decay that even embalming can’t stop. For decades, the practice has been growing in popularity as a more environmental and space-saving way to prepare bodies after death.

But that’s not the end of the story. Traditional cremation requires temperatures of 1,400–1,600 Fahrenheit, the Cremation Association of North America explains. The type of ashes we imagine—where what is left is fine powder with some small shards of bone—is just not possible with a wood fire. While it is possible with coal or maybe an accelerant, at that point, the environmental catch-22 is pretty evident. Traditional cremation is better at saving space than it is at saving the planet—and saving space has had enormous value around the world for thousands of years.

The Financial Times estimates that each traditional cremation in the U.K. in 2018 cost about 150 kilograms of carbon dioxide; that’s more than a one-way flight from Boston to Paris. Traditional funerals cost many thousands of dollars on average, and burying embalmed human bodies in airtight containers has never been an environmentally friendly project to begin with. If you’re thinking about your future, there are more options than ever.

At Return Home, the “immediate need” package costs $5,950. The organization also offers another option at the same price: pre-planning your funeral and financing it with a payment plan. At Recompose, the composting service is $7,000, with options for various remembrance services ranging from $500 up to $1,700. These are somewhat in line with current funeral costs, estimated at an average of $8,596, according to US Funerals Online, an industry resource company based in Delaware.

There’s also one wrinkle if you want your body to be composted after your death: Bodies cannot be embalmed before the process starts. The chemicals used in the funeral industry are “not compatible with” the natural decomposition process, Recompose explains, and many are carcinogenic or otherwise toxic. In other words, they aren’t safe to mix into soil that people will take home and use in their yards. If you die while traveling, you will typically be embalmed before you’re transported home.

There’s an interesting split over human composting, particularly evident in Christianity. The Verge’s 2022 article about Return Home leads with an anecdote about Sharon, a woman who had died from complications of multiple sclerosis. She was also a Mormon. True-blue Christians hew to an idea called stewardship, which is the way humankind must care for the earth and environment as cornerstones of God’s creation.

And today, that often includes climate change. According to a 2025 survey from Pew Research Center, highly-religious Americans are more likely to believe God gave humans the duty to protect Earth, even in comparison to those who are moderately religious. However, there is also a history of cremation being a contentious issue in Catholicism, though the strictness has relaxed in recent years. Taboos about burial did not stop Sharon, and perhaps won’t stop others who don’t take the resurrection of the body literally. To many people, even those who are Christians, the body is the vessel for what really makes human beings special.

Your reaction to the details above might be a good litmus test for how you feel about human composting. But if you think it sounds disgusting, and to even think about it is macabre—that’s valid! The vast majority of Americans are still choosing traditional burial or cremation. Today, human composting is legal in more than a dozen states, with legislation in the process in several more.
